crumbs.name: AI Adoption and Governance in Life Sciences

reading.body:
Drugmakers are co-developing AI agents that sit inside research platforms and assist scientists, with Owkin building such agents under a multiyear collaboration with Sanofi.

The pattern is partnership rather than procurement. A research organisation does not buy a finished agent and install it. It co-develops the agent with an outside party, which means the agent is shaped around the internal research platform it will live in. That is a different adoption path from a general-purpose model dropped into a workflow.

For AI specifically, the constraint this exposes is not compute but data rights. An agent that assists scientists learns from the platform it sits in. Who owns what it learns is a question that has to be settled before work starts, not after. The one governance instruction attached to this case is exactly that: agree data rights and ownership of what the agents learn before co-development begins.

The data covers one announced collaboration and one governance recommendation. It does not say how many agents were built, what they cost, what compute they run on, or whether they worked. It names no other drugmaker and no other vendor. Treat it as a single documented instance of a co-development model, not as evidence about how widespread that model is.

siblings.name: Governing AI in a Regulated Company

explainer:
Research organisations are building AI agents that work inside their own platforms: searching internal and public data, running analyses, summarising results and suggesting next steps for scientists. Some are developed with specialist AI companies under multiyear collaborations.

Co-development raises questions worth settling first: who owns the agents and the improvements they learn from company data, whether the partner can reuse anything with other clients, how data are protected, and how the agents will be validated where their outputs feed regulated work.
